\caption[]{Measured response of the transcriptome to a gene deletion. \textbf{``Responding'' means $|\log_2$ FC$| > \log_2 1.25$}, that is, a gene whose expression moved by more than 1.25-fold in either direction relative to wild type, on the array platform of the source compendium. There is no significance test behind it and none is available per gene per strain: the criterion is a magnitude cut on the reported log ratio, applied identically to all three datasets. A single deletion moves a few hundred genes by that criterion but only $\sim$10--15 by 2$\times$, so designing at two-fold targets a few percent of the response. \textbf{The 1.34$\times$ in the last column is conditioned on that cut and is not independent of it.} The $|\Delta|$ distribution falls off monotonically (\cref{fig:effect-size}a), so the median of whatever upper tail is selected sits just above the cut that selected it: the same statistic is 1.16$\times$ at a 1.1$\times$ cut, 1.36$\times$ at 1.25$\times$, 1.73$\times$ at 1.5$\times$ and 2.57$\times$ at 2$\times$ (\cref{fig:effect-size}c, right axis). What the column establishes is therefore not a natural effect size but a consequence of choosing 1.25$\times$, and the choice is what to argue with. It matters because the power coefficient $A$ scales as $|\Delta|^{-2}$, so at 1.34$\times$ every cell requirement is $\sim$5.6 times the two-fold figure. Doubling the perturbation count roughly doubles the responder count at 1.25$\times$ and trebles it at 2$\times$, without shifting the median response -- more perturbations make a cell noisier, not its individual effects larger. Generated from \file{experiments/024-perturb-seq-costing/scripts/effect_size_analysis.py}.}\label{tab:effect-size}
